title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Introduction
content: The lymphatic system is a complex component of the immune system that plays a crucial role in filtering substances throughout the body. Lymphocytes are the integral agents involved in searching for target proteins and travel through lymph nodes, which are diffusely placed throughout the body. Lymphadenopathy refers to the swelling of lymph nodes. Lymph nodes are small glands that are responsible for filtering fluid from the lymphatic system. They are divided into sections known as follicles, which are further subdivided into B zones and T zones, representing the base location of lymphocytic maturation.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Abnormal proliferation of lymphocytes may be a result of inflammation, infection, or malignancy; therefore, clinicians must perform a detailed history and physical examination to screen for lymphadenopathy. When inspecting for lymphadenopathy, one should carefully examine all pertinent anatomic regions, including the neck, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions. In general, the size of a normal lymph node in the adult population should be less than 1 cm; however, there are exceptions to this rule. [1]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Lymphadenopathy, while pertinent, may be nonspecific. There are several potential causes of lymphadenopathy, ranging from infectious, autoimmune, malignant, and lymphoproliferative.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Etiology
content: There is a wide range of infectious etiologies, including bacterial, fungal, viral, mycobacterial, spirochetal, and protozoal organisms. Autoimmune disorders that may contribute include, but are not limited to, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Malignant diseases like lymphoma, leukemia, metastatic cancer, and head and neck cancers are also common causes of lymphadenopathy. Lymphoproliferative disorders such as hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis can also manifest with the enlargement of lymph nodes.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Lymphadenopathy can be localized or diffuse. Approximately 75% of lymphadenopathies are localized, and about 50% of these occur in the head and neck regions. Generalized lymphadenopathy, which involves two or more non-contiguous regions, is reported to occur in 25% of lymphadenopathies. [2]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Elucidating the etiology of lymphadenopathy can be a challenging task. A thorough history and physical examination are among the most important steps in determining the underlying cause of lymphadenopathy.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Etiology
content: Etiologies can be determined based on lymph node groups. Submental and submandibular lymphadenopathy is commonly infectious in origin, often presenting with viral prodromes. Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy can arise from localized bacterial and viral infections, as well as lymphoma. [2] Axillary lymphadenopathy can also be related to lymphoma or breast malignancy, but can also be caused by infections such as cat-scratch disease. Lastly, inguinal lymphadenopathy can be impacted by local sexually transmitted infections, lymphoma, and pelvic malignancies.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: A majority of patients with lymphadenopathy will have a benign etiology. Age is a crucial factor in characterizing the epidemiology of lymphadenopathy, and thus, it can be divided into two categories: children and adults.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Children more commonly appear to have benign causes of lymphadenopathy. To better understand this, a study completed by Knight PJ et al reviewed 239 children who underwent a peripheral node biopsy and found that the most common etiology noted was reactive hyperplasia of unknown etiology, followed by granulomatous infections, cancer, and dermatopathic lymphadenopathy. [3]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: Adults also appear to have a low prevalence of malignancy. To further characterize this, a study was completed in a family practice setting where only 3% of 249 patients with lymphadenopathy underwent biopsies. Of these patients, no one was found to have a debilitating illness. [4]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: A Dutch study also revealed that of 2556 patients who presented with unclear lymphadenopathy to their family physicians, 10% were referred for a biopsy, and only 1.1% were found to be related to malignancy. These findings are mirrored by two case series conducted in family practice departments within the United States, which demonstrated that 0 of 80 patients and 3 of 238 patients had malignant causes of lymphadenopathy, respectively. It is important to remember that endemic regions such as South Africa or India have increased rates of lymphadenopathy due to tuberculosis, parasitic infections, and HIV. [2]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Lymph nodes are a part of the reticuloendothelial system, which includes monocytes in the blood, macrophages in the connective tissue, the thymus, spleen, bone marrow, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue in visceral organs, lymphatic vessels, and lymphatic fluid found in interstitial fluid. [1]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Lymphatic fluid moves throughout the lymphatic system, transitioning from the organs to lymphoid capillaries, lymphatic vessels, and ultimately to lymph nodes for the filtration of foreign antigens. Foreign substances are presented to the lymphoid cells, which leads to cellular proliferation and enlargement. Under microscopy, cellular proliferation in lymphoid follicles can be identified by the presence of several mitotic figures. [5] As lymphatic capsules stretch due to increased activity, patients may experience localized tenderness.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The development of B-cells originates from pluripotent stem cells from the bone marrow. B cells that successfully assemble their immunoglobulin heavy chains migrate to the germinal centers, allowing for antibody diversification through somatic hypermutation. [6] B-cell lymphomas are believed to result from alterations in somatic hypermutation and chromosomal translocations.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The development of T-cells also begins from pluripotent stem cells, which mature within the thymic cortex. [7] While in the thymic cortex, T cells begin specific rearrangements at the T-cell receptor. It is understood that chromosomal translocations affecting the T-cell receptor level lead to T-cell lymphomagenesis.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: Lymph node follicle necrosis may occur as a result of various conditions, including inflammatory, infectious, or malignant conditions. The predominance of neutrophilic infiltrates suggests a bacterial infection, while a lymphocytic predominance may suggest a viral infection. However, clinicians must remember that etiologies may vary; lymphomas, leukemias, tuberculosis, or even systemic lupus may be more appropriate diagnoses in the appropriate clinical context. [8]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Histopathology
content: Bacterial lymphadenitis: Predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate can be found within the sinus and medullary cords. Follicular hyperplasia can also be observed. [9] [10] Viral lymphadenopathy: Infiltration by macrophages and lymphoid hyperplasia. Necrosis can be seen in those who are immunocompromised. [11] Sarcoidosis: Non-caseating granulomas that replace the normal architecture of the lymph node Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: There is partial or widespread loss of the lymph node by a single cell lineage. Lymphoid cells can either proliferate in a disorderly manner or as those that mimic follicular center structures. Hodgkin lymphoma: Can be classified by the histological appearance noted below. These histological types are listed in order from most common to least common. [12] Nodular-sclerosing Mixed cellularity Lymphocyte-rich Lymphocyte-depleted

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Physical examination involves the following: Vital signs, including temperature, Blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation, are all significant in determining if the patient is hemodynamically stable. This can help differentiate sepsis from benign conditions. A head-to-toe exam must be conducted, including inspection of the head, ears, nose, throat, and thyroid gland—auscultation of lungs, heart, and palpation for splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. A thorough inspection of the skin should be performed, palpating when necessary, to look for rashes, lesions, and nodules. When palpating lymphadenopathy, it is essential to consider the location, size, firmness, and pain.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: Location: Anterior cervical lymph nodes are superior and inferior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Posterior cervical lymph nodes are posterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. One should also inspect for supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy bilaterally. Local lymphadenopathy suggests a more localized disease as compared to widespread lymphadenopathy. [1] Size: Cervical lymph nodes and axillary nodes are atypical if > 1 cm, as compared to supraclavicular > 0.5 cm, and inguinal nodes >1.5 cm. Firmness: Generally, if a lymph node is readily mobile, it is less concerning for a malignant condition. Pain: Pain can be a sign of inflammation, an acute reaction to an infection, or a less concerning sign of a malignant process.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Listed below is a diagnostic approach that may help clinicians evaluate lymphadenopathy: Laboratory evaluation: blood chemistries including complete blood count with differential, complete metabolic panel, lactate dehydrogenase, fungal serologies (histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcosis), laboratory evaluation of Syphilis, HIV, CMV, EBV, HSV, HBV, QuantiFERON for tuberculosis. Imaging: Computed Tomography (CT) scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis can be used to substantiate further the location, pattern, and size of lymphadenopathy. This can also guide a biopsy if needed. [14] Lymph node biopsy: The need for a lymph node biopsy depends on the etiology of lymphadenopathy. An excisional node biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing lymph node involvement. [15]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Treatment differs depending on the etiology of lymphadenopathy. Simply put, the following generalizations can be made: Malignant: Surgery +/- radiation therapy +/- chemotherapy. Autoimmune: Immune therapy, systemic glucocorticoids. Infectious: Antibiotic therapy, antiviral therapy, or antifungal therapy. Medication: Discontinuation of medication with re-evaluation is necessary.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Infectious: Many different infections can contribute to benign changes in the lymph nodes. Health care providers may consider several different subcategories of infection, including bacterial, viral, and other: Bacterial: brucellosis, cat-scratch disease, bacterial pharyngitis, syphilis, tuberculosis, tularemia, typhoid fever Viral: cytomegalovirus, hepatitis, herpes simplex, HIV, mononucleosis, rubella, viral pharyngitis. [16] Other: bubonic plague, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, toxoplasmosis

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Staging
content: Staging is a process in oncology that enables healthcare providers to determine the extent of disease burden from its primary locations. It should be known that malignant lymphadenopathy can occur from both primary lymphomas and from metastatic cancer. Most, but not all, cancers use the tumor, node, and metastasis (TNM) staging system. A tumor refers to the primary involvement by the neoplasm, as well as the depth of the participation. Nodes describe the local lymph nodes involved in the disease process, and metastasis refers to distant sites where the disease spreads. The staging of non-Hodgkin and Hodgkin lymphoma is based on the Lugano classification, which is based on the Ann Arbor system. [17]

content: Stage I: Lymphoma found in 1 lymph node or in only one lymphoid organ Stage II: Lymphoma is found in 2 or more groups of lymph nodes on the ipsilateral side of the diaphragm Stage II: Lymphoma involvement bilaterally in reference to the diaphragm Stage IV: Lymphoma has metastasized to one organ beyond the lymphatic system

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: Generally, lymph node enlargement in younger populations (for example, children) tends to be benign and usually related to infection. There are exceptions to the rule, particularly if the patient’s history and physical are concerning for chronic infection, malignancy, or autoimmune conditions. Other risk factors that may be poor prognostic indicators include, but are not limited to, advanced age, length of duration of lymphadenopathy (> 4 weeks is concerning), generalized lymphadenopathy, male sex, lack of resolution of node size, and systemic signs (such as fever, night sweats, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly). [18]

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Complications
content: While lymphadenopathy itself may not lend itself to complications, unaddressed lymphadenopathy may lead to worsening progression of an underlying condition, the most concerning of which is sepsis or metastatic cancer. For lymphadenopathy related to autoimmune disorders, progressive autoimmune disease may lead to cancer or dysfunctional immunity, which may lead to significant morbidity and mortality.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education remains critical in mitigating concerning lymphadenopathy. Abating interactions with modifiable risk factors such as alcohol, environmental toxins, recreational drugs, and/or tobacco may significantly reduce the risks of malignant lymphadenopathy. Immunizations and safe sex practices may help reduce the risk of infectious lymphadenopathy.

title: Adenopathy(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Healthcare providers, including nurses, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and physicians, all need to be aware of the significance of lymphadenopathy. Most cases of lymphadenopathy are nonspecific; therefore, the provider caring for a patient needs to be aware of these signs, in addition to advising patients to monitor for any abnormal growths or inconsistencies in regional lymph node sites.
